---
title: "Polling-Place Closures and Voter Turnout"
abstract: |
  What is the causal effect of polling-place closures on voter turnout? This question matters because unequal access to polling locations may distort democratic representation. We estimate the effect using a difference-in-differences design based on staggered county closures from 2012 to 2020. Relative to prior studies of travel distance and turnout, we contribute nationwide precinct-level evidence and a design that isolates within-county changes. We find that a closure reduces turnout by approximately 1.8 percentage points, with larger effects in low-income precincts.
---

# Introduction

The section opens by explaining why equal access to polling places matters for democratic representation. It states the primary question: what is the causal effect of a polling-place closure on precinct-level turnout?

## Main contribution

The paper contributes nationwide precinct-level evidence on closures and turnout and estimates within-county changes rather than relying on cross-sectional comparisons.

## Relationship to prior research

Prior studies examine travel distance, voter identification laws, and local case studies. We explain how our national panel, closure measure, and staggered design differ from those approaches.

# Theory and hypotheses

The main message is that closures increase voting costs. H1 predicts lower turnout after a closure. H2 predicts a larger decline in low-income precincts. These implications will be tested using precinct turnout and census-derived income measures.

# Data

The population of interest is voting-age citizens in United States precincts from 2012 through 2020. The analysis combines state election returns, polling-place records, and American Community Survey data. The outcome is precinct turnout as a share of voting-age citizens. Key explanatory variables are closure exposure, post-closure status, and neighborhood income.

# Research design and identification

We use staggered difference-in-differences with county and election fixed effects. Identification requires parallel untreated turnout trends and no closure-timed confounders. Event-study estimates will assess pre-trends; placebo closure dates and covariate balance checks will evaluate assumption plausibility. Threats include selective closures, precinct-boundary changes, and concurrent election-administration reforms.

# Results

The section opens with the estimated average treatment effect of a closure on turnout. The primary estimand is the percentage-point change in precinct turnout. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate a decline of approximately 1.8 percentage points, followed by tests of heterogeneous effects by neighborhood income.

## Robustness and sensitivity

We will compare alternative treatment-timing estimators, exclude precincts with boundary changes, vary fixed effects, run placebo timing tests, and report sensitivity to differential pre-trends.

# Conclusion

The conclusion relates reduced turnout after closures to equitable election administration and states the limits of extrapolating beyond observed counties.

# Replication appendix

De-identified analysis data, variable-construction documentation, and replication code will be deposited in a public repository. The appendix will provide estimator details and additional diagnostics.
